o: A substring can be rearranged into a palindrome exactly when AT MOST ONE digit occurs an odd number of times — pairs fold symmetrically around the center and a lone odd count sits in the middle. Only parities matter, so keep a 10-bit mask where bit d records whether digit d has appeared an odd number of times; prefix masks combine via XOR, giving mask(l..r) = pre[r] XOR pre[l-1]. In example 1 ("3242415") the substring "24241" has even counts of 2 and 4 with a single 1, hence one odd digit — awesome, length 5. The task becomes: find two prefix positions whose masks are equal (even-length palindromes) or differ in exactly one bit (odd-length), as far apart as possible. With n up to 10^5 only near-linear algorithms survive.
k: Palindrome-feasibility depends solely on count parities, so a 10-bit mask summarizes any substring.
mask(l..r) = pre[l-1] XOR pre[r]; the substring is awesome iff these masks match or differ in a single bit.
Remembering only the FIRST occurrence of each mask lets every index resolve in O(10), yielding O(10n) overall.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Running Parity Mask
a.i: Fix the left endpoint and sweep the right one, updating a running XOR mask and testing whether its popcount is at most 1. Correct and a useful correctness reference, but quadratic — hopeless at n = 10^5.
s: Extend r from l onward, XORing bit (s[r] - 0) into mask.
When popcount(mask) <= 1 update the best length r - l + 1.
a.t: O(n^2 * 10) — all substring endpoints with a popcount check per step.

a.n: Approach 2: First Occurrence of Every Prefix Mask
a.i: Record the earliest index at which each of the 1024 possible masks appears (with mask 0 seeded at index -1 for the empty prefix). Walking left to right, at index r the current mask either was seen before — giving an even awesome substring — or matches some mask differing in one digit bit, giving an odd one; storing first occurrences maximizes both lengths. Ten bit-flip probes per index keep the whole scan linear.
s: Seed map first[0] = -1; maintain running mask starting at 0.
At each i XOR bit (s[i]) into mask.
If mask was seen, candidate length i - first[mask]; otherwise store first[mask] = i.
For each digit d probe first[mask ^ (1 << d)] and take that candidate too.
a.t: O(10 * n) — each index does constant work plus ten fixed probes.
a.sp: O(1024) = O(1) — one entry per possible mask.

w: Lead with the parity reduction — it converts a palindrome question into bitmask bookkeeping. Pitfalls: forgetting the empty-prefix seed mask 0 (misses substrings anchored at index 0), testing only exact mask equality and losing all odd-length answers, and tracking full counts instead of parities. Edge cases: single characters (1), all identical digits (n), ten distinct digits like "12345678" (1). Follow-ups: the same technique solves LeetCode 1371 over a 26-letter alphabet (5 extra bits) and variants asking to COUNT awesome substrings or support letter substitutions.
